blocks.text: One mole of hydrogen weighs 2 g. One mole of carbon dioxide weighs 44 g, twenty-two times as much. Yet at the same temperature and pressure both occupy exactly the same volume. That surprising fact makes gas calculations far easier than they look.

blocks.title: Avogadro's law
blocks.text: Equal volumes of all gases, measured at the same temperature and pressure, contain equal numbers of molecules. It follows that the volume occupied by one mole is the same for every gas under the same conditions.

blocks.markdown:
## Molar volume

The **molar volume** is the volume occupied by one mole of any gas.

- At s.t.p. (273 K, 760 mmHg): **22.4 dm3/mol**, that is 22400 cm3/mol
- At room temperature and pressure (about 298 K, 1 atm): approximately 24 dm3/mol

WAEC and NECO questions use 22.4 dm3 at s.t.p. unless they tell you otherwise.

$n = \dfrac{\text{volume of gas at s.t.p. in dm}^3}{22.4}$

The reason the identity of the gas does not matter is that gas molecules are so far apart that their own size and their attractions are negligible. What fills the container is empty space, and that space depends only on how many molecules there are.

blocks.caption: Same volume, same number of moles, very different masses

blocks.markdown:
### Gay-Lussac's law of combining volumes

When gases react, the volumes of the reacting gases and of any gaseous products bear a **simple whole-number ratio** to one another, provided all volumes are measured at the same temperature and pressure.

Because of Avogadro's law, that ratio is exactly the mole ratio in the balanced equation. So for gases only, you may work directly in volumes without converting to moles at all.

N2(g) + 3H2(g) -> 2NH3(g)

1 volume of nitrogen + 3 volumes of hydrogen -> 2 volumes of ammonia.

blocks.title: Combining volumes in a combustion
blocks.prompt: 10 dm3 of methane is burned completely in oxygen. All volumes are measured at the same temperature and pressure. Calculate the volume of oxygen used and the volume of carbon dioxide produced.

steps.text: Write the balanced equation: CH4(g) + 2O2(g) -> CO2(g) + 2H2O(l).
Note that water is a liquid at room temperature, so it contributes no gas volume.
By Avogadro's law the gaseous mole ratio CH4 : O2 : CO2 of 1 : 2 : 1 is also the volume ratio.
No conversion to moles was needed, because every quantity is a gas measured under the same conditions.

blocks.answer: 20 dm3 of oxygen is used and 10 dm3 of carbon dioxide is produced

blocks.markdown:
### Vapour density

The **vapour density** of a gas is the ratio of the mass of a volume of the gas to the mass of an equal volume of hydrogen measured under the same conditions. Since hydrogen is diatomic with a relative molecular mass of 2,

**relative molecular mass = 2 x vapour density**

A gas with a vapour density of 22 therefore has a relative molecular mass of 44, which fits carbon dioxide.

blocks.title: Two traps in gas volume questions
blocks.text: First, check the state symbols. Water produced in a combustion is a liquid at room temperature and must not be counted as a gas volume. Second, if a question quotes a volume in cm3, convert to dm3 by dividing by 1000 before using the 22.4 figure.

points: Equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules.
One mole of any gas occupies 22.4 dm3 at s.t.p.
Moles of gas equal the volume in dm3 at s.t.p. divided by 22.4.
For gaseous reactants and products, the volume ratio equals the mole ratio in the balanced equation.
Relative molecular mass is twice the vapour density.
